title: Decades After Its Silver Screen Days, My Cobra Was Returned to Its Original Glory

body_markdown:
My Cobra has always been a part of my life. Dad purchased it in 1975, the same year I was born. Before he owned it, the car, serial number CSX2038, had been rented by MGM Studios for[the Elvis movie](https://www.hagerty.com/media/entertainment/new-elvis-movie-is-a-buffet-of-the-kings-cadillacs/) *Viva Las Vegas* and *The Killers* with Ronald Reagan, and was also used by the Carroll Shelby School of High Performance Driving.


*Welcome to the[Hagerty Movies and Cars Celebration](https://www.hagerty.com/media/magazine-features/welcome-to-the-hagerty-movies-and-cars-celebration/) , where we highlight and explore the relationship between[cars and the silver screen](https://www.hagerty.com/media/tags/movies-and-cars/) .*


The Cobra wasn’t in great shape when he bought it—it was in gray primer, with a sparse racing dash, short windshield, and side pipes. Dad owned a successful automotive repair shop in Fresno, California, so he and his crew restored and customized the car. He painted it Rangoon Red, fitted flared fenders and chrome 6-inch-wide wire wheels. He added a chrome roll bar and a custom-made chrome front bumper. By that time, the original 260-cubic-inch V-8 was long gone, replaced by a 289 with Cobra valve covers, Ford blue engine paint, and lots of chrome. Dad showed the car in 1978 and ’79 and won concours events in Fresno and Palo Alto.


Hanke’s Cobra has been in his family for a half-century, since his father purchased it and repainted it in Rangoon Red (right).


Courtesy Brandon Hanke


Hanke’s father showed the Cobra at concours events in the late 1970s (middle right).


Courtesy Brandon Hanke


In 1980, I was riding in the passenger seat and we were speeding down Belmont to Dad’s shop for work. I remember a bang, then smoke began pouring into the passenger compartment. The 289 blew a rod. For the next 45 years, the car sat in the garage. My brother and I used to take turns sitting in the black leather seats, pretending to drive. We begged Dad to build a motor and bring the Cobra back to life, but he always had something more important to do. In 2003, Dad was invited to Carroll Shelby’s 80th birthday at[the Petersen Museum](https://www.hagerty.com/media/tags/petersen-automotive-museum/) in Los Angeles, so we polished the Cobra and trailered it down. That was a great day; I had never imagined I’d get to see so many Cobras in one place.


Dad unexpectedly passed in fall 2022, and my brother and I were left with his incredible collection of cars, motorcycles, and automotive memorabilia. Since I was the oldest son, I was always promised the Cobra by Dad. I wanted to get the car back on the road, so I did a little research and decided to bring the car to Drew Serb, a Shelby expert and owner of the[Cobra Experience](https://cobraexperience.org/) museum in Martinez, California.


A full recent restoration returned the Cobra to its original white-over-red livery.


Courtesy Brandon Hanke


The car had hidden damage from its time at MGM Studios and Shelby’s racing school, so Serb and I decided it was best to strip the car to its frame for a full nut-and-bolt restoration. We decided to take the car back to its original condition, too: slab-side fenders, five painted wire wheels, white exterior with red interior. One exception we did make was with the engine. We decided to install a 289, exactly as Dad had. (I do have a 260 in the garage just in case.)


Three anxious years later, the car was complete. Now the car is stunning. My wife and I have taken it to a few local shows and are hoping to attend some concours events soon. The best is when someone asks if it’s real. My reply is always a confident, “Yes, it is.”


Courtesy Brandon Hanke
